docs.surfaced.component: `Surfaced` is the atom that draws. Give a node a surface and it becomes visible; without one
it still exists, it just has nothing to show.
```ts
import { node, Bounded, Surfaced, registerSurface } from "game-kit"
registerSurface("plate", {
layers: [{ paint: "panelBg" }],
radius: 0.08,
stroke: { color: "accent", width: 0.03, alignment: 1 },
const card = node("card", Bounded(), Surfaced({ surface: "plate" }))
registerSurface("plate", { layers: [{ paint: "panelBg" }] })   // every plate loses its border, at once
## The field
One: `surface`, the name of a registered record. Not the colours themselves.
There used to be two more — `fit` and `align`, how a picture meets the area it is given.
They were declared before a record had layers or pictures at all, so nothing ever read them:
two controls a reader could move to no effect whatsoever. They belong to the layer, where a
picture and an area actually meet, and they come back with the picture.
## Why a name and not the colours
Re-register a record and every node using it changes in one step, while no box moves. The
name also keeps the wire short and stable: `"plate"` is the same string on every client,
whereas a palette copied into each message is state two clients can legitimately disagree
about — and a saved game would reopen in last year's colours.
An unregistered name is skipped rather than thrown. A dangling reference is a content
mistake, and failing the whole scene over one would hide every node that was fine.
## What a record holds
- `layers` — coats of paint over the area, bottom first. Each is a colour, a picture, or a
colour under a picture. A list rather than one fill, because the cases stack for real: a
tiled ground with an emblem over it is two layers and cannot be said with one.
- `radius` — how the contour's corners are rounded, in units.
- `stroke` — the border, drawn last. `color`, `width`, `opacity`, `alignment`, `cap`, `join`,
`miterLimit` and a `dash` pattern.
The names are the renderer's, which are also SVG's and Canvas2D's. A record is a PROXY of the
renderer's style rather than a dictionary of our own: a smaller vocabulary loses whatever it
leaves out, and the loss is invisible until somebody needs the field that was dropped.
Two things are deliberately not passed through. Lengths are in UNITS, never pixels — a border
given in pixels is a different border on every screen. Colours are TOKEN NAMES, not literals
— a GPU canvas has no cascade to resolve a variable in, and a backend with no CSS at all
resolves the token against its own palette. Everything else is plain data, which is what lets
a record cross a wire or a language boundary.
## A border is not a picture of a border
Stretch the area and the stroke does not stretch with it. Its width and its dash lengths are
absolute, so what changes is the NUMBER of dashes, never their size. That falls out of the
unit rule rather than being a setting: the stroke is an operation on the contour, computed
when it is drawn, not an image scaled to fit.
The dash pattern carries SVG's two adjustments. `adjust: "stretch"` (the default) scales the
period so a whole number of them fits the contour — without it the first and last dash meet
at the start point and read as one dash of double length, which is the documented artifact
`stroke-dashadjust` was added to SVG to fix. `corner: "dash"` repeats the pattern per side,
so every corner is covered by a dash instead of whichever gap the walk happened to land in.
## Where the area comes from
A surface needs an area, and there are two sources for it: the node's own box (`Bounded`) or
the extent of its content (`Container`). Either satisfies the requirement — this is the atom
that made requirements alternatives in the first place. Demanding `Bounded` would rule out
the desk, which has plenty to paint and no footprint of its own.
## Pictures
A layer's `image` is a registry reference, like the surface's own name — `registerAsset` says
where the picture comes from and how big it is MEANT to be, **in units**.
The declared size is not a formality. Fitting a picture into an area needs its proportions,
and if those only arrived when the file had downloaded, the geometry would depend on the
network and no test could check it. Declared up front, it is arithmetic — the plan is right
before a single byte lands, and the renderer redraws when the picture catches up.
`fit` and `align` live on the LAYER, because that is where a picture and an area meet. One
setting on the node could not describe a ground tiled `repeat` and an emblem in a corner at
the same time, and those are one record.
- `contain` (the default) — the whole picture, letterboxed if the proportions differ.
- `cover` — fills the area and overflows; the contour clips what hangs over.
- `fill` — the only fit that distorts, and it says so in its name.
- `original` — drawn at the size the asset declared.
- `repeat` — that same size, tiled.
- `fitX`, `fitY` — one axis followed, proportions kept.
`contain` is the default deliberately. `cover` always looks tidy and quietly eats the edges,
so a picture with the wrong proportions ships and nobody notices; `contain` makes a wrong
result look wrong, which is the only kind of wrong that gets fixed.
One more thing worth trying: switch the theme. A layer painted with a TOKEN follows it; a
picture does not, and neither does a literal colour. That is the difference the palette is for.
docs.surfaced.plate: `Bounded`'s own box, one atom later, and now you can see it.
Everything the model can hold is here: any shape the box can be — a rect, a circle, a polygon
of as many corners as you like, or one pasted in from a design tool — and every property of
the record, down to `cap`, `join` and both of the dash adjustments.
That is on purpose, and it is a correction. This scene used to be a rectangle with a colour
picker, and a separate one showed three fixed shapes with no record at all. A reader could not
tell what the kit cannot do from what the catalog did not ask — so the two are one scene, and
nothing is narrowed.
The controls are the RECORD's, not the atom's: the atom has one field, and it is the name this
record is registered under.
Things worth doing here:
- switch the dash on and stretch the box. The dashes multiply; not one changes size. Then set
`dashAdjust` to `none` and look at the top-left corner: the first and last dash meet there
and read as one long one. That is why `stretch` is the default.
- set `alignment` to `0` with a wide border and turn on `bounds` in the toolbar: the stroke
hangs outside the box the layout carefully spaced from its neighbours.
- pick a picture, then walk `fit` through its values on a circle. `contain` letterboxes,
`cover` overflows and is clipped by the contour, `repeat` tiles.
- put a literal colour in `fillCustom`, then switch the theme. The token would have followed;
the literal does not.
docs.surfaced.path: One node, and the smallest interesting thing a surface can be asked to paint: a path.
The places are `from` and `to`, and they are yours to move. `bend` is a number: at zero the
run is straight, and above it the middle is pulled sideways while both ends stay where they
were. There is no switch anywhere that says «straight» or «curved», and there is not going
to be one — a curve is where a path's places are, and `bend` puts one between the ends.
A shape is a REGION, so the path closes itself: walked out and walked back it encloses
nothing, the fill has nothing to cover, and everything visible is the stroke. That is the
whole record below — the same one `Plate` builds, doing less because there is less to do.
A line is a path and a stroke and nothing more. Put a head on it and you have an arrow, and
that is an ASSEMBLY of two such nodes rather than a cleverer line: it lives on
docs.surfaced.arrowHead: The other half of an arrow, on its own — because that is what it is: one node, one shape,
The shape comes out of a registry by name. `pointer`, `begin`, `stop` and `diamond` are the
stock four; a fifth is a `registerHead` call with any closed shape at all behind it, which
is why a suit or a piece is not a special case and needs nothing added here.
Unlike the path before it, THIS shape has an inside — so the fill is doing something, and
the same record can make the head solid, hollow, or a box with a picture on it. That is the
whole reason a head is its own node rather than a detour in the line's contour: one node
wears one record, and an arrow usually wants two.
`turn` is the angle a path arriving at that angle would give it. On its own a head knows
nothing about paths — `Presets/Components` is where the two meet.
docs.surfaced.zone: A surface on a node with no box of its own. The area comes from what the node HOLDS — which
is what the alternative requirement is for — widened by `padding` around the tight wrap of
it. Take padding to zero and the surface shrinks to exactly that wrap; take the children away
and there is nothing left to paint on at all.
`children` is a REAL list, one entry per node, edited as the object it is — not a count this
scene expands into anonymous boxes. Every id typed here lands on the node exactly as written;
nothing here renumbers or overwrites what a reader put in the panel. The one exception is a
blank id, filled the same way every node's own `id` control is on every other page in this
kit — and it is an exception worth naming, not a silent default.
`gap` and `padding` both belong to the ROW rather than to this node: spacing is a parameter
of the arrangement, never a field the container itself would have to carry for the one
layout in five that could actually use it.
docs.surfaced.starved: `Surfaced` with neither a box nor content: the atom is on the node and there is no area to
Nothing is drawn, and nothing is wrong. A starved atom is a legal state, not an error — the
tree below reports `Surfaced` as unsatisfied, and the node goes on existing. Give it a box
and it appears, with the same record it had all along.
